label: Eisenhower Runs As A Democrat
detail: The famous general seeks the presidency under the banner of the party in office since 1933 instead of the party out of the presidency since 1933.
assumption: The party out of the presidency since 1933 nominates a different candidate, while the general carries his personal popularity and moderate stances into the ballot of the party in office since 1933. Voters respond to his personal appeal while the party labels shift.
facts_text: Both major parties had courted the general in 1948 and 1952, and the party in office since 1933 would have welcomed him as its standard-bearer.
The President, having decided not to seek another term, supports the general's candidacy on the ticket of the party in office since 1933.
nominee_news: He had been courted by both major parties before deciding which nomination to seek, and he has made clear his wish to see the party in office since 1933 continue its foreign policy.
The general, recently commander of allied forces in Europe, has accepted the nomination of the party in office since 1933 after it was pressed upon him.
research_questions: How did voters who admired the general as a war hero split by party loyalty in 1952 when party labels and personal popularity conflicted?
In 1952 how many Southern and urban voters of the party in office since 1933 would have stayed loyal to a candidate of their own party who was a famous nonpartisan figure?
In similar elections where a popular war hero changed party, how much of his personal vote followed him?
source_text: Dwight Eisenhower runs for president as a Democrat in 1952.
